content: 1. The term S is an abbreviation that stands for not otherwise specified. 2. For detailed information regarding non-infectious GMOs or GMMOs, refer to the United Nations model regulations. 3. Proper shipping names for medical or clinical wastes may vary depending on the mode of transport. It is essential to consult applicable regulations to determine the correct shipping name. 4. Materials or products that are non-pathogenic, inactivated, or neutralized through decontamination processes (e.g., autoclaving or incineration) are not considered to pose a health risk and are therefore not subject to transport regulations unless they meet the criteria for dangerous goods in another classification. 5. Examples of complete exemptions include: Cultures containing biological agents that are non-pathogenic to humans or animals. Patient specimens for fecal occult blood screening or dried blood spot testing. Biological products such as blood or blood products for transfusion, or body parts for transplantation. Medical or clinical waste that has been appropriately decontaminated using methods like autoclaving or incineration. Medical equipment that has been drained and confirmed to be free of any contaminated liquid. 6. Specimens such as food, soil, or water shipped for investigational purposes, which are not considered to pose an infection risk to humans or animals, also fall under this definition. 7. When transported by air, exempt specimens must be packaged using a basic triple packaging system. This system includes: A leak-proof primary receptacle. A leak-proof secondary packaging. An outer packaging of sufficient strength for its capacity, mass, and intended use, with at least one surface having minimum dimensions of 100 mm × 100 mm. 8. For liquids, absorbent material in sufficient quantity to absorb the entire contents must be placed between the primary receptacle(s) and the secondary packaging to prevent leakage from reaching the outer packaging or compromising the cushioning material. 9. Once contained in an appropriate triple packaging system, exempt specimens are not subject to additional infectious substance regulations. 10. Professional judgment is required to determine whether a patient specimen qualifies as exempt, based on known medical history, symptoms, individual circumstances of the source (human or animal), and endemic local conditions. 11. Exempt human or animal specimens must be packaged in the same basic triple packaging system described for air transport, regardless of the mode of transport. 12. The outermost layer of the package must be marked with the words Exempt Human Specimen or Exempt Animal Specimen, as appropriate. 13. Properly marked and labeled exempt specimens are considered safe for transport and are not subject to further infectious substance regulations. 14. Used medical devices or equipment potentially contaminated with infectious substances must be packaged to prevent breakage, puncture, or leakage under normal transport conditions. 15. Such packaging must be marked with the words Used Medical Device or Used Medical Equipment, as appropriate. 16. This exception does not apply to: Medical waste (UN 3291 and UN 3549). Medical devices or equipment contaminated with Category A infectious substances (UN 2814 or UN 2900). Medical devices or equipment contaminated with other dangerous goods that meet the definition of another hazard class. 17. Infectious substances are defined as materials reasonably expected to contain biological agents capable of causing disease in humans or animals. 18. Classification of infectious substances must be based on the material's composition and the level of risk it poses to human or animal health. 19. Infectious substances capable of causing severe harm, such as permanent disability or life-threatening disease, are classified as Category A. 20. Category A substances are assigned to UN 2814 (affecting humans) or UN 2900 (affecting animals only). 21. Category B infectious substances, which pose a lower risk, are assigned to UN 3373 with the proper shipping name Biological Substance, Category B. 22. Medical or clinical wastes containing Category B infectious substances are assigned to UN 3291. 23. Accurate classification and assignment of UN numbers and proper shipping names require professional judgment, especially for new or emerging pathogens. 24. Packaging for infectious substances must be of high quality and strong enough to withstand challenges during transport, such as movement, vibrations, and changes in temperature, humidity, and pressure. 25. Infectious substances must be contained in a triple-layered packaging system with redundant layers and sufficient absorbent material to control leaks or breaches. 26. Specific packing instructions, such as P620 for Category A substances and P650 for Category B substances, outline detailed requirements for safe transport. 27. The use of dry ice as a coolant for infectious substances transported by air must comply with additional packing instructions, such as PI954 in the ICAO Technical Instructions. 28. Infectious substances must not be transported as hand carriage on passenger aircraft, even in diplomatic pouches. 29. Materials defined as Exempt Human Specimen or Exempt Animal Specimen can be transported in a triple-layer packaging system across all modes of transport.
